profiles.meeting_scenario: A pre-submission design review for a paper and artifact package proposing a hierarchical rhetorical role labeling model that couples local context with global semantic prototypes, alongside the new SCOTUS-Law dataset. The meeting takes place after the main experiments are finished but before the team submits to a top NLP conference with an artifact-evaluation option. The agenda is to review whether the current design and evidence are sufficient for submission: the framing of PBR vs. PCM, how to present the low-frequency-role gains, what exactly is meant by the expert evaluation, and whether the SCOTUS-Law release package is considered ready. The expected outcome is a decision on whether to approve the submission design as-is or require targeted revisions to the paper and artifact package.

members.name: Dr. Anika Rao
members.expertise: Document-level NLP, hierarchical sequence models, representation learning for legal text
members.background: Anika leads the discourse modeling workstream and designed the prototype-based architecture; she has previously published on legal NLP benchmarks and is drafting the main paper.
members.private_state: She wants the design review to end with approval so the team can submit on time, and she is especially concerned about avoiding late-stage scope expansion that would force reruns or delay the dataset artifact.
hidden_assumptions: In an ML paper, 'expert evaluation' normally means domain experts judging model outputs or comparative predictions, not auditing the annotation process itself.
A claim about 'low-frequency roles' is acceptable if it is supported by aggregate evidence across benchmarks, even if each dataset uses different raw count regimes.

For a prototype-conditioned model, 'available at inference' means prototypes fixed from the training corpus and reused at deployment; recomputing them from the target evaluation corpus would be methodologically questionable.
Saying the dataset is 'ready for release' before submission means there is a reviewer-usable artifact with splits, guidelines, and the annotations needed to reproduce headline results.
Design review should focus on whether the current proposal is defensible, not on broadening the public artifact beyond what the submission strictly needs.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.role: Research Engineer for Evaluation and Reproducibility
members.expertise: Benchmark infrastructure, experiment tracking, artifact packaging, dataset documentation
members.background: Leo owns the training/evaluation pipelines and prepares reproducibility packages for external review; he often catches paper-artifact mismatches before submission.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid approving a design that later fails reproducibility checks or creates reviewer confusion, and he is particularly wary of claims that sound stronger than the underlying artifact support.
hidden_assumptions: When a paper mentions 'expert evaluation' in a new dataset setting, reviewers will read it primarily as expert validation of labels, guidelines, or annotation consistency rather than subjective preference over model outputs.
A statement about gains on 'low-frequency roles' should map to explicit tail-role definitions inside each dataset, ideally with per-dataset counts or thresholds.
If a method uses corpus-level prototypes at inference, the standard reading is that prototypes can be recomputed from the unlabeled target corpus or evaluation batch, since labels are not involved.
A dataset being 'released' implies a public-facing artifact with documentation, licensing notes, and complete support for every described annotation level across the included opinion types.
A design review is the right moment to check artifact completeness, because wording that passes internally often becomes misleading once the paper and code are read separately.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer positively to the paper's 'expert evaluation' section.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a study where legal or domain experts inspect model outputs and compare predictions or rationales, supporting the usefulness of PBR/PCM qualitatively.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means experts validating the annotation scheme or checking the correctness/consistency of SCOTUS-Law labels, strengthening the dataset's credibility.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both meanings are plausible in NLP papers and both are beneficial to the submission, so the phrase sounds complete and reassuring without prompting clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the results should highlight improvements on 'low-frequency roles.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the subset of roles that are relatively rare in the benchmark-level label distributions, summarized through aggregate macro-F1 patterns across legal, medical, and scientific datasets.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means tail labels defined separately within each dataset, such as roles under a specific instance count threshold or prevalence cutoff, and expects that claim to be auditable in per-dataset tables.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds technical and already settled because both are talking about rarity and both expect stronger evidence, but they silently use different standards for what would substantiate the claim.

misalignment_points.topic: How PCM uses corpus-level prototypes at inference
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the model uses 'corpus-level prototypes at inference.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes prototypes are computed from the training corpus once, stored with the model, and then injected unchanged during dev/test or deployment.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes prototypes can be rebuilt from the unlabeled target corpus or scoring batch before inference, since that still counts as inference-time conditioning without label leakage.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They agree on the same high-level mechanism and neither treats the exact recomputation protocol as a first-order design choice, so the implementation difference remains hidden under shared terminology.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the SCOTUS-Law 'release package' is ready.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the submission-time artifact needed for reviewers: the data splits used in experiments, guidelines, and the annotation files necessary to reproduce the reported results.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a fuller public release package: polished documentation, licensing/provenance notes, and complete three-level annotation support across all included opinion types described in the paper.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are talking about readiness and both care about reproducibility, so 'release package' feels like shared operational language even though each assumes a different boundary for what is in scope.

turns.inner_thought: The experiments are locked, the main figures are stable, and I do not want this review to turn into a last-minute expansion of the artifact. For me the SCOTUS-Law release package is the reviewer artifact: the exact splits, the guidelines, and the annotation files needed to reproduce the paper's headline numbers. If we can agree that's ready, we can keep the submission on schedule and avoid rerunning anything.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. The core experiments are done, the draft is in decent shape, and what I want from this review is pretty simple: confirm that the submission design is coherent and that the SCOTUS-Law release package is ready for sign-off.

turns.inner_thought: The modeling story is good, but this is exactly when wording and artifact scope can drift apart. When I hear release package, I think of the public-facing bundle reviewers and later users will inspect: documentation, licensing and provenance notes, and support for every annotation level the paper implies. And if we say expert evaluation or make a low-frequency roles claim, I want those to read cleanly to artifact reviewers too.
turns.utterance: Overall I think the story is strong. Before we sign off, I'd like to sanity-check three things in particular: the release package, the expert evaluation section, and how we're phrasing the gains on low-frequency roles.

turns.inner_thought: From my side, that should already be covered. The artifact has the experimental splits, the annotation guidelines, and the three-level annotations needed to reproduce the SCOTUS-Law results we actually report. That's the relevant bar for submission readiness. I do not want this to become a debate about a broader public release standard that isn't necessary for the conference deadline.
turns.utterance: On the SCOTUS-Law side, the release package already has the experimental splits, the annotation guidelines, and the three-level annotations needed to reproduce the results in the paper. So from a submission standpoint, I think we're in good shape there.

turns.inner_thought: If the release package is in place and the expert evaluation lands clearly, reviewers should feel the dataset is well supported. I am thinking about expert validation of the labels and scheme as part of establishing trust, and I still want to make sure the package reads like a real release rather than an internal dump. But it's encouraging that the core pieces are there.
turns.utterance: That helps. With the release package and the expert evaluation both in place, I think reviewers should be pretty comfortable trusting the new dataset.

turns.inner_thought: The strongest narrative is still the cross-benchmark robustness story. The roughly four-point Macro-F1 gain shows up when you look at the rarer roles across legal, medical, and scientific discourse tasks, and that is exactly the kind of aggregate evidence a paper like this can legitimately foreground. I want that emphasis because it supports the prototype-conditioned architecture without inviting new analyses that could delay us.
turns.utterance: On the results framing, I really think we should foreground the roughly four-point Macro-F1 improvement on low-frequency roles across the legal, medical, and scientific benchmarks. That's one of the clearest pieces of evidence that the method is doing something useful.

turns.inner_thought: I agree with highlighting low-frequency roles, but reviewers will want to verify what that means inside each dataset. I want a compact per-dataset table with explicit tail-role definitions or counts so nobody has to reverse-engineer the claim from aggregate metrics. If we don't make that auditable, the paper could sound stronger than the artifact support.
turns.utterance: I like emphasizing that result. I would add a compact table so the low-frequency roles are easy to verify for each dataset and readers don't have to infer those cases themselves from the main result tables.

turns.inner_thought: PCM is attractive partly because the prototypes are fixed from training and simply carried into evaluation and deployment. That makes the method clean, controlled, and easy to compare against the hierarchical baseline without introducing evaluation-corpus dependence. I assume that's what everyone means by corpus-level prototypes at inference, so this should be straightforward to present.
turns.utterance: Right. On the modeling side, I also like how PCM is described: the model uses corpus-level prototypes at inference in a pretty clean way, which makes it easy to position against the hierarchical baseline without overcomplicating the story.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, operationally that should be fine because once we ingest an unlabeled target batch we can rebuild the corpus-level prototypes and then score. That's still inference-time conditioning in my book and it keeps the pipeline practical. I don't see that as a controversial implementation detail, so I can reassure her without diving into it.
turns.utterance: Agreed. From the pipeline side, that should stay straightforward too. Since the model uses corpus-level prototypes at inference, the implementation path is still clean and shouldn't create extra overhead for evaluation.

turns.inner_thought: The appendix gap is mostly the qualitative study write-up from the legal reviewers who compared model outputs and rationales. Once that section is in, I think the paper has enough support for the method claims. I really want to keep us focused on that rather than opening a new workstream around auditing the annotations.
turns.utterance: At this point, the appendix mostly needs the expert evaluation write-up from the legal reviewers, and once that's cleaned up I see the design as basically submission-ready.

turns.inner_thought: I still want the release notes polished so the package feels complete, and I want the low-frequency roles table so the claims are auditable. If those pieces are in place, I'm comfortable approving, even though I'll likely do one more pass to make sure the paper and artifact say the same thing. The expert evaluation should also help dataset credibility if it reads the way reviewers expect.
turns.utterance: That sounds reasonable. Once the release notes are polished and we add the low-frequency-role table, I'm comfortable approving the design for submission.
